Reentrancy.engineer: Classical reentrancy: an external call returns control to an attacker contract before the calling function has finished updating its state. The attacker re-enters the same or a related function while the protocol still believes the prior call has not completed, executing the path repeatedly against stale balances. Modern variants include cross-function reentrancy (re-entering a sibling function that shares storage) and read-only reentrancy (manipulating a view function that another protocol trusts). The Curve 2023 incident generalised this further: compiler-emitted reentrancy locks themselves can be wrong.
Reentrancy.founder: Reentrancy bugs typically drain the affected pool to zero in a single transaction. The headline is straightforward: 'protocol drained, $X lost'. Recovery is almost never possible without a fork or a goodwill return. Reentrancy is also the attack class most users have heard of, so a reentrancy bug is reputationally costly even if the dollar loss is modest.
Reentrancy.sigmaPrime: Sigma Prime engagements treat reentrancy as a class problem, not a function-by-function checklist. We trace every external call in the system to confirm state mutation precedes the call, including calls to attacker-controllable tokens and oracles. Echidna or Foundry invariants assert that 'no sequence of legal calls leaves balances inconsistent with deposits'. Compiler-version pinning and bytecode-vs-source verification are deliverables for any Vyper or non-standard-Solidity codebase.

Access Control.engineer: Access-control failures cover privileged functions reachable by an unintended caller (uninitialized owners, missing onlyOwner modifiers, bypass paths like donate-to-reserves, or token-mint authorities held by an EOA). The Parity 2017 freeze and Euler 2023 drain share a single root cause: a state-modifying function was reachable by code paths that bypassed the standard checks. Modern variants include fake-LP and fake-mint attacks where a privileged setter or minter is callable on a freshly created pool or token.
Access Control.founder: The dollar number on these is usually large because the attacker is not exploiting a subtle bug, they are exercising a function that was always intended to drain or mint, just not by them. Recovery depends entirely on whether the attacker is identifiable, in which case law enforcement or social pressure may help, or whether the funds have already moved through mixers, in which case the loss is final.
Access Control.sigmaPrime: Sigma Prime audits enumerate every privileged role and every code path that can reach a state-mutating function. We require timelocks on any function that can change the privileged set or upgrade the implementation, and we assert (with fuzzers) that no sequence of legal calls bypasses the standard health or balance checks. EOA-owned minter and upgrade roles are flagged as critical findings regardless of the rest of the codebase's quality.

Oracle Manipulation.engineer: An attacker uses cheap, atomic capital (often a flash loan) to move a price on a low-liquidity reference market, then borrows against the inflated collateral or sells into the deflated market. The classical 2020 bZx variant used a single Uniswap v1 spot price; the Cream 2021 variant used a yield-vault share price inflatable by a direct transfer; the Mango 2022 variant pumped a thinly-traded perp. The common thread: a price source that can be moved within the same transaction as the action it secures.
Oracle Manipulation.founder: Oracle-driven hacks tend to drain the collateral pool entirely. The loss number is bounded by the size of the borrowable assets, not by the attacker's capital. Headlines for these incidents emphasise the cleverness of the attacker rather than the negligence of the protocol, which makes recovery via legal channels harder than for access-control or key-compromise events.
Oracle Manipulation.sigmaPrime: Sigma Prime treats every external price source as a trust-path question. Spot DEX prices are not trusted for collateralisation. Chainlink and similar feeds get reviewed for staleness windows, deviation thresholds, and circuit breakers. Vault share prices used as collateral must have a virtual-offset (ERC-4626) defence or a hardcoded floor. The threat model is delivered as a written document, not a checklist.

Flash Loan.engineer: Flash loans are not the vulnerability, they are the funding mechanism. A flash loan turns 'attacker needs $50M of capital to manipulate the system' into 'attacker needs $0 of capital and one block'. The actual vulnerability is almost always an oracle, an invariant bypass, or a governance shortcut elsewhere in the stack. Reviewing 'flash-loan defence' in isolation is a category error.
Flash Loan.founder: Flash-loan-funded attacks reach full scale instantly. There is no early-warning period in which a defender can pause the contracts. The full possible loss happens in the same transaction the attacker decides to act. Insurance and DAO-vote responses are too slow.
Flash Loan.sigmaPrime: Sigma Prime invariants are asserted at end-of-transaction, not block-end. We fuzz with the explicit assumption that the attacker has unlimited atomic capital, and we ask 'does any legal sequence with infinite capital break this invariant?' If the answer is yes, the protocol is unsafe regardless of normal liquidity depth.

Bridge.engineer: Bridges combine the worst of both worlds: a contract surface and an off-chain validator/signer infrastructure, both of which must be perfectly secure simultaneously. The contract side has had spectacular failures (Nomad's zero-root upgrade, Wormhole's missing instruction check). The off-chain side has had even bigger ones (Ronin's compromised validator quorum, Multichain's centrally-held MPC shares). A bridge audit that only covers the contracts is a bridge audit that misses 50% of the surface area.
Bridge.founder: Bridge hacks are the largest losses on record. Ronin, Wormhole, Nomad, Multichain, Orbit, Bybit cold-wallet, all crossed the $100M line. Recovery is rare and usually depends on the attacker being a known state actor (Lazarus) or a project with capital to backfill (Jump for Wormhole). The brand damage is permanent.
Bridge.sigmaPrime: Sigma Prime engagements for bridges include the validator infrastructure, key custody, rotation cadence, signing-flow UI, and operational runbooks alongside the contracts. A cryptographer is added to the team for any cross-VM or threshold-signature work. Validator-set rotation paths are timelocked and fuzz-tested. We require hardware-display verification of full calldata for every privileged signature.

Key Compromise.engineer: Key compromises range from pure social engineering (phishing a signer, SIM-swapping a custodian, hiring a Lazarus operator who implants a backdoor) to operational supply-chain attacks (compromised Safe-Wallet UI, malicious CI scripts, leaked HSM material). The contract layer is irrelevant; the security perimeter is wherever the signing key actually lives.
Key Compromise.founder: These are usually the worst-impact, fastest-execution incidents. Once the attacker has the keys, the entire treasury is drained in minutes. Public communications matter more than technical response, because there is no technical response left to make.
Key Compromise.sigmaPrime: Sigma Prime treats custody review as a distinct deliverable from contract review. We assess hardware isolation, geographic distribution of signers, rotation cadence, signing-UI provenance, second-channel hash verification, and the operational runbook for break-glass procedures. Sign-what-you-see attacks (Radiant 2024, WazirX 2024, Bybit 2025) are now table stakes to defend against.

Frontend / Supply Chain.engineer: The smart-contract perimeter ends at the user's browser. Attackers compromise DNS providers, CDN accounts, CI/CD pipelines, signing UIs, or NPM dependencies, and inject JavaScript that rewrites approval targets or replaces displayed calldata. BadgerDAO 2021 was the first famous example (Cloudflare key compromise); Bybit 2025 was the most expensive (Safe-Wallet UI tampering).
Frontend / Supply Chain.founder: These incidents are easy to underestimate because 'our contracts are fine'. They are not fine if the dApp users see is signing different transactions than the one displayed. Recovery depends on how fast the malicious frontend can be killed and how many users approved before that happened.
Frontend / Supply Chain.sigmaPrime: Sigma Prime engagement scoping asks about CSP headers, subresource integrity, DNS and CDN account hardening, signer-display patterns (Permit2, blind-signing warnings), and dependency-pinning. For multisig-managed protocols we require hardware-only calldata display and an independently-built signing UI used in parallel for diff-comparison before any production signature.

Governance.engineer: Governance attacks use governance-token concentration (flash-loaned or otherwise acquired) to pass a malicious proposal. The Beanstalk 2022 incident is the canonical case: flash-loan the threshold of stake, propose a treasury-draining BIP, vote yes, execute in the same block. Variants include compromised multisig signers (which technically is key compromise but routed through governance), and delegate-spoofing in Snapshot.
Governance.founder: These are reputationally devastating because the protocol's own decentralisation mechanism was used against it. The dollar number is bounded by what the governance contract can move, which for most modern DAOs is the full treasury.
Governance.sigmaPrime: Sigma Prime governance review requires a non-zero voting window (so flash-loaned voting weight cannot both be acquired and exercised inside one transaction) and a timelock between acceptance and execution. We flag any path where governance-token balance is what gates execution rather than time-weighted stake.

Rug Pull.engineer: Rug pulls are intentional, not accidental. The contract author deploys a token or protocol with a hidden privileged path (mint, blacklist, fee-on-transfer, withdrawal-disabler), waits for adoption, then drains. The technical work is usually trivial; the social work (building trust, getting listed, attracting liquidity) is the actual operation.
Rug Pull.founder: If you are reading this as a victim, recovery is rare. If you are reading this as someone considering adopting an unaudited token, the absence of a publicly identifiable team and a credible audit is the warning sign you are looking for.
Rug Pull.sigmaPrime: Sigma Prime does not audit contracts deployed by anonymous teams without strong, verifiable real-world identities. An audit cannot prevent intentional malice by an authorised actor; it can only verify that no unauthorised actor has the same capability.

Invariant.engineer: Invariant failures are the protocol-level analogue of access-control bugs: a sequence of legal calls leaves the system in a state that violates a property the rest of the system depends on. Euler 2023's donateToReserves let an attacker put themselves underwater without triggering the standard health check, then self-liquidate. KyberSwap Elastic 2023's tick-rounding bug let liquidity be counted twice. The bug is never one function; it is the interaction of two.
Invariant.founder: Invariant losses tend to be large because the protocol's bookkeeping has gone wrong, and every action taken against the wrong books deepens the hole. Recovery depends on whether the protocol can be paused before too many users transact against the broken state.
Invariant.sigmaPrime: Sigma Prime invariant-based review is the deliverable here. Echidna and Foundry harnesses assert system-wide properties: solvency, monotonicity of accumulators, conservation of tracked assets. We do not stop at 'this function reverts on bad input'; we assert 'no legal sequence of inputs leaves the protocol in a state where any actor can extract value asymmetrically'.

Infrastructure.engineer: Infrastructure compromises include cloud-provider database breaches (Mixin 2023), CI/CD pipeline tampering, dependency-injection attacks, and HSM operator-workstation compromise. The smart contracts are not exploited; the off-chain systems holding the signing material or the database of user balances are.
Infrastructure.founder: These are deeply unsexy from a marketing standpoint. There is no clever exploit to dissect; an admin password leaked or a cloud account was misconfigured. The technical narrative is uninteresting, the dollar loss is real, the public response usually undersells the severity.
Infrastructure.sigmaPrime: Sigma Prime infrastructure review covers the full key-derivation path: where seeds come from, where they are stored at rest, who has access at the cloud-provider level, and how rotation works. A clean smart-contract audit means nothing if signing keys live in an unaudited storage bucket.

Other.engineer: Insufficient detail in the upstream data to classify this incident into a specific attack class. The live feed records name, date, loss, and chain, but not always a technique label. Treat this entry as a placeholder pending hand-curation.
Other.founder: Live-feed entries without a technique classification should be treated as raw signal that an incident occurred. Read the linked post-mortem (or the project's own disclosure) before assuming anything about the cause.
Other.sigmaPrime: Once technique details emerge, this entry will be promoted to a curated entry with the full engineer / founder / TAM narrative and a references[] array citing every consulted source. See CLAUDE.md for the promotion process.
